notes:
Below are my notes on Genesis 14, verse by verse. A few things to know first. I couldn't reach several sites. **I found nothing from the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) or the Orthodox one (oca.org), and nothing written by prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers themselves.** The NET Bible notes below come from quotes on the Precept Austin page, not from netbible.org directly. The Precept Austin page cut off partway through v. 6, so my notes for vv. 6–24 rely on other sources.

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Guzik says these four were kings of city-states, not rulers of large regions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/ The Ryrie Study Bible (quoted by Precept Austin) reads Shinar as Babylonia and Elam as what later became Persia. It says Amraphel should not be identified with Hammurabi, who lived later, and that Goiim's location is uncertain. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-14-commentary Precept Austin itself admits archaeology hasn't firmly identified these kings, but holds that they really existed because Scripture says so. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64221/ It also calls this the first war in the Bible. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64221/

**v. 2:** The NET note (via Precept Austin) says the war fits Bronze Age practice: overlords ruled vassal city-states, and treaty partners joined each other in battle. It reads this as Chedorlaomer's war against western cities that had stopped paying tribute. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-14-commentary)

**v. 3:** Precept Austin notes that the tar pits mentioned in v. 10 suggest the Valley of Siddim was known for asphalt. Henry Morris (quoted there) thinks the words "the Salt Sea" may be an editorial note added by Moses. He argues the area was still fertile and well watered in Abram's day. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-14-commentary)

**v. 4:** For Guzik, the five kings' revolt after twelve years of submission is what set off the invasion. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/) The NET note sees the story as a preview of Israel's later troubles with eastern empires, like Hezekiah's revolt against Assyria. Its lesson for later readers was that God can give victory over tyrants from the east. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-14-commentary)

**v. 5:** Henry Morris links the Rephaim, Zuzim and Emim to giant peoples, the Anakim. He goes further and suggests demonic involvement. That is his own reading, not a common one. Wiersbe, citing Ezekiel 16:49–50, suggests that Sodom's soft way of life left it unready for war. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-14-commentary)

**v. 6:** The NET note traces the route: down the east side of the Jordan Valley into the desert, then back up the valley toward the cities of the plain. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-14-commentary)

**v. 7:** Guzik says the four kings attacked several tribal groups, then the Amalekites and Amorites, all living south of the Dead Sea. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/)

**v. 8:** Guzik thinks the five kings joined the fight because they wanted to be free of Chedorlaomer's rule. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/

**v. 9:** Coffman (Restoration Movement) reads the new order of names as a ranking by importance. Since Amraphel is now near the bottom, Coffman argues he was no great world ruler. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/14-9.html

**v. 10:** Guzik, quoting Leupold, says the Hebrew repeats "pits, pits of bitumen" to show how many there were. He also cites the archaeologist Nelson Glueck on ruined villages along the invaders' path. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/)

**v. 11:** Precept Austin notes that "they" means the four kings. Captives must also have been taken, since in v. 21 the king of Sodom asks for his people back. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-14-commentary

**v. 12:** Guzik quotes Spurgeon: believers who conform to the world must expect to suffer for it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/ Precept Austin calls Lot's capture God's discipline, a reminder that he had no business living in Sodom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-14-commentary Jamieson, Fausset & Brown teach that leaving the path of duty puts us outside God's protection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_014.cfm

**v. 13:** There are several explanations of "Hebrew":
- Guzik says this is the word's first use in the Bible and probably refers to Abram having "passed over" the Euphrates. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/)
- Barnes notes that the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) translates it as "one who passes." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/14-16.html
- Matthew Henry takes it to mean a descendant and follower of Heber (Eber), whose family kept the true faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/14-16.html
- A footnote on Bible.org mentions a possible link to the Habiru, who often worked as mercenary soldiers. https://bible.org/seriespage/rescue-lot-genesis-141-24

Henry also guesses that the escapee was probably a man of Sodom who hoped Abram would help for Lot's sake. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_014.cfm

**v. 14:** For Guzik, the 318 men show Abram's great wealth. They also show that a man of faith can be prudent and keep a trained force ready. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/ Jamieson, Fausset & Brown note that Abram refused to repay Lot's ingratitude with evil. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_014.cfm

**v. 15:** Guzik credits Abram's military skill: a night attack with his force split in two. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/ The Biblical Illustrator contrasts this courage with Abram's fearfulness in Egypt (12:12–13). It says he fought "by faith." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/genesis-14.html The same commentary says God usually works through means rather than miracles. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/genesis-14.html

**v. 16:** Matthew Henry says Abram rescued even the people of Sodom, strangers he owed nothing. The lesson is to do good to all people as we have opportunity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_014.cfm Guzik and Bible.org both see the rescue as a picture of salvation: a kinsman leaves his safety to free a captive relative. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/ https://bible.org/seriespage/rescue-lot-genesis-141-24 Guzik adds that Lot went back to Sodom anyway. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/

**v. 17:** The Biblical Illustrator describes Abram's triumphant return with Lot, his men and the freed captives. It calls this first recorded war a triumph of right. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/genesis-14.html)

**v. 18:** Guzik makes these points (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/):
- The text never explains where Melchizedek came from.
- His name means "king of righteousness," and Salem was the original Jerusalem.
- Holding both king and priest roles was unusual. God later forbade this in Israel; Uzziah was struck with leprosy for trying (2 Chronicles 26).
- The bread and wine may look ahead to the Lord's Table.

The Bible Hub study notes call the meal hospitality for tired men, a sign of fellowship after the victory, and also a pointer to the covenant meal Christ instituted. https://biblehub.com/genesis/14-18.htm

**v. 19:** Seedbed points out that Melchizedek blesses Abram, not the other way round. It says the title El Elyon ("God Most High") appears 28 times in the Old Testament. https://seedbed.com/abraham-meets-the-king-priest-melchizedek/ https://seedbed.com/abraham-meets-the-king-priest-melchizedek/ Guzik notes that a priest serves in both directions: he blessed Abram, and he blessed God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/)

**v. 20:** Several writers explain the tenth:
- Gill says it came from the enemy's spoils, not from the recovered goods, which went back to their owners. https://www.studylight.org/bible/fin/rat/genesis/14-20.html
- Barnes sees it as Abram admitting that Melchizedek's God was supreme and his priesthood genuine. https://www.studylight.org/bible/fin/rat/genesis/14-20.html
- Utley (Bible.org) calls it Abram's way of thanking God and admitting that God won the victory. https://bible.org/series/passage.php?page=1829
- Seedbed says it was customary to give a king a tenth of the spoils. https://seedbed.com/abraham-meets-the-king-priest-melchizedek/
- Bible Hub connects the verse to Hebrews 7:9: Levi, Abraham's descendant, in a sense paid the tithe through him, so the Levitical priesthood ranks below Melchizedek's. https://biblehub.com/hebrews/7-9.htm

**v. 21:** Matthew Henry says the king of Sodom had first claim to his people and goods. He sees the offer as a fair proposal to avoid a quarrel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_014.cfm Wiersbe (quoted by Precept Austin) sees a subtle temptation instead. Egypt's wealth had already been a snare, and Sodom's would have been worse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-14-commentary

**v. 22:** Guzik notes that Abram uses "God Most High" right after hearing Melchizedek use it. "Raised my hand" means he had made a vow. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/ Utley points out that Abram puts the LORD and God Most High side by side as the same God. https://bible.org/series/passage.php?page=1829 Jamieson, Fausset & Brown also read "lifted up mine hand" as swearing an oath. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_014.cfm

**v. 23:** Guzik says Abram wanted all credit for his wealth to go to God alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/ The Biblical Illustrator adds that God had made Abram heir of the land, so he would not take any of his inheritance from a man, least of all from Sodom's king. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/genesis-14.html G. Campbell Morgan says the refusal shows how high Abram's faith was. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-14-commentary

**v. 24:** Guzik notes that Abram did not push his own principles on his Amorite allies. They could take their fair share by the custom of the day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/

## Where views differ

**v. 18 (Who was Melchizedek?)**
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Sinclair Ferguson says most of the panel believe Melchizedek was an ordinary human king. "Without father or mother" means no family line is recorded, not that he wasn't human. https://learn.ligonier.org/qas/was-melchizedek-a-preincarnate-appearance-of-jesus-christ https://learn.ligonier.org/qas/was-melchizedek-a-preincarnate-appearance-of-jesus-christ
- **Gospel Coalition:** Don Carson is "thoroughly unconvinced" that this was an appearance of Christ. He sees a link of type and picture instead, and calls the Christophany idea a fundamental mistake. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/Revelation-part-20/ https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/Revelation-part-20/
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Guzik leaves it open. If Melchizedek wasn't Jesus himself, he was at least a remarkable picture of Christ. He dismisses other guesses (Shem, Job, an angel) as having no biblical basis. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/)
- **GotQuestions:** says a case can be made either way. https://www.gotquestions.org/Melchizedek.html
- **NET note (via Precept Austin):** Some identify him with Christ or with Shem. The note thinks it far more likely he was a Canaanite royal priest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64221/
- **Early church:** Precept Austin cites Jerome's report that Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Eusebius and others saw Melchizedek as a man. Most Reformers agreed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_71-3

**v. 18 (Bread and wine)**
- **Methodist (Seedbed):** calls bread and wine basic elements of life that would "reemerge" at the Passover and the Eucharist. https://seedbed.com/abraham-meets-the-king-priest-melchizedek/
- **Restoration Movement (Coffman):** Coffman quotes an early reading of the meal as a picture of the Lord's sacrifice. Willis called that "fanciful," saying it was just food for tired men. Coffman pushes back: Abram already held all the spoils and didn't need food. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/14-18.html
- **Barnes:** thinks a sacrifice was probably offered through Melchizedek before the meal. https://www.studylight.org/bible/fin/rat/genesis/14-20.html

**v. 20 (Is tithing binding on Christians?)**
- **Enduring Word:** Guzik says the tithe principle predates the Law of Moses. The New Testament stresses giving in proportion (1 Corinthians 16:2), and a tenth can be treated as a goal. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-14/)
- **Bible Hub Q&A (strongest view):** treats the tithe as "the floor, not the ceiling." It answers the objection "we are under grace" by saying grace raises the standard. It also says that, by Malachi 3:10, withholding the tithe forfeits promised blessings. This is the nearest I found to blessing-focused teaching, but it isn't a prosperity-teacher source. https://biblehub.com/q/Applying_Genesis_14_20_tithing_today.htm https://biblehub.com/q/Applying_Genesis_14_20_tithing_today.htm https://biblehub.com/q/Applying_Genesis_14_20_tithing_today.htm
- **Bible.org (on Hebrews 7):** stresses that Hebrews uses the tithe to show the rank between the two men, "not as a fund-raising device." https://bible.org/seriespage/16-abraham-melchizedek-and-messiah-hebrews-71-10

## Other views

**v. 1 (Is the chapter historical?)**
- **Older critical scholarship (Peake's Commentary):** Inscriptions don't confirm the invasion, the five kings, Abraham or Melchizedek. Experts disagree on who the four kings were. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/genesis-14.html Peake allows that Melchizedek may have been historical. Jerusalem's priests and kings may have claimed him as a forerunner. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/genesis-14.html
- **Catholic Encyclopedia:** says Babylonian records from Hammurabi's time fit what Genesis 14 assumes. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01441a.htm
- **Bible Hub topical article:** calls the Amraphel–Hammurabi link the best proposed so far, though with difficulties. https://biblehub.com/topical/a/amraphel.htm
- Ryrie (under v. 1 above) rejects that identification.

**vv. 18–20 (Catholic)**
- Catholic Answers: Melchizedek is not Jesus but a prefiguring of him. It describes him offering "a sacrifice of bread and wine." https://www.catholic.com/qa/was-melchizedek-jesus
- Catholic Answers magazine: calls the bread and wine one of two Eucharistic pictures in Genesis. It notes Melchizedek's offering is remembered in the First Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-eucharists-long-shadow-across-the-bible

**Jewish (Dead Sea Scrolls)**
- Precept Austin notes that the Qumran scrolls (Cave 11) present Melchizedek as a coming deliverer and link him with the archangel Michael. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_71-3
